name: Outcome independence
summary: Caring about the person and the moment while not needing a particular result from the interaction.
how_to_apply: Set the goal as 'enjoy this and be myself' before the conversation; treat a no or a lukewarm response as information, not a verdict.
example_line: Either way, I've enjoyed this. You're good company.
markers: pitch_median_hz and speaking_rate_wpm stable after a rejection or flat moment
no persuasion or re-asking after a decline
common_mistakes: Using 'outcome independence' as an excuse not to show interest
drill: Before each social event write one process goal (e.g. 'three follow-up questions') and score only that afterwards.

name: Spot and drop covert contracts
summary: Noticing when niceness is secretly a trade (I'll be lovely, so you'll like me) and replacing it with open requests and honest giving.
how_to_apply: Before a favour, compliment or agreement, ask: would I do this if it earned nothing? If not, either ask directly for what you want or don't do it.
example_line: I'd like to see you again. Are you up for that?
markers: over-agreeing (agreement tokens with no own view)
requests framed indirectly rather than asked
common_mistakes: Swinging to rudeness to prove you're not nice
Keeping score silently and resenting her
drill: For one week, log each time you did something hoping for a hidden payoff; for each, write the direct ask you could have made.

name: Say your real opinion
summary: Sharing genuine preferences and disagreements instead of mirroring what you think she wants.
how_to_apply: When asked what you think, answer with your actual view in one sentence, then ask hers; disagree warmly when you disagree.
example_line: Honestly? I think brunch is overrated. Fight me.
markers: certainty_per_100w up, hedges_per_100w down on opinion turns
agreement tokens ('totally', 'same') immediately after her opinions
opinions that flip when she disagrees
common_mistakes: Lecturing once you've stated a view
drill: In three conversations, state one mild, genuine disagreement and keep it friendly; note her reaction.

name: Stop approval-seeking tags
summary: Removing verbal habits that ask for reassurance, like 'is that weird?', 'does that make sense?' and 'sorry, I'm rambling'.
how_to_apply: End points with a full stop and a pause instead of a check-in; let her respond on her own.
example_line: That's why I moved to Lisbon. (pause)
markers: count of 'does that make sense', 'is that weird', 'sorry I'm rambling'
common_mistakes: Replacing tags with long silence that feels cold
Removing all checks, including genuine ones about her comfort
drill: Record a 2-minute story; tally every reassurance tag; redo with zero and compare.

name: Purpose first
summary: Building a life organised around a mission he cares about, so a woman joins his world rather than becoming its centre.
how_to_apply: Keep commitments to your own projects even when dating is going well; talk about what you're building with genuine energy.
example_line: I'm deep into building this product. It's eating my weekends, and I love it.
markers: energy (pitch_range_st, loudness_sd_db) rises when discussing his own work
common_mistakes: Using purpose as a reason to be unavailable or dismissive
drill: Write one paragraph on what you're building this year; practise saying the 20-second version with energy.

sources.where: women as part of a full life

name: Don't make her the mission
summary: Avoiding pedestalising: treating one woman as the prize or main life goal before you know her.
how_to_apply: Keep investment in step with what you actually know about her; keep friends, hobbies and plans intact in the early weeks.
example_line: I'm away climbing on Saturday, but I'm free Sunday evening.
markers: talk about rearranging plans for her
drill: After a good date, list three non-dating things you'll do that week and do them.

sources.where: don't put her first too early

name: Selective, specific interest
summary: Showing interest in her in particular, rather than being enthusiastic about everyone, which research links to being desired back.
how_to_apply: Compliment and ask about specific things she said or chose; don't gush generically.
example_line: The way you talked about restoring that bike, that's the most alive you've looked all night.
markers: references to earlier details she gave
drill: After each interaction write one specific thing you liked; say that kind of thing next time.

name: Honest expression of interest
summary: Telling her plainly that you're attracted or want to see her again, accepting the risk of rejection.
how_to_apply: Once you feel it and she's engaged, say it once, warmly, without a question tag; then let her respond.
example_line: I like you. I'd like to take you out properly.
drill: In your next three dates, state your interest once, clearly, before the end.

name: Vulnerability as a mindset
summary: Being willing to show real feelings, flaws and wants without performing; strength shown by not hiding.
how_to_apply: Share one real thing that matters to you, briefly, then return the floor; don't use vulnerability to fish for sympathy.
example_line: I was nervous coming here, which is funny because you're very easy to talk to.
drill: Once per date, share one honest feeling in the moment in a single sentence.

name: Polarise rather than please
summary: Expressing your real personality so that some people like you a lot and some don't, instead of everyone feeling lukewarm.
how_to_apply: Show genuine tastes, humour and opinions early; read a mismatch as a successful filter.
example_line: I'm a total morning person. If you hate sunrises, this may be a dealbreaker.
common_mistakes: Being abrasive and calling it polarising
drill: Name three genuine tastes you usually hide and mention one per conversation.

name: Warm-up before you go out
summary: Getting into a sociable, talkative mood before the important conversation rather than starting cold.
how_to_apply: Have a few easy chats (barista, friends) before the date or event; music and movement help.
example_line: (Habit: three small chats en route.)
markers: opening-minute loudness_db and pitch_range_st vs his baseline
common_mistakes: Overly hyped energy that doesn't match hers
drill: Before your next social event, have three brief friendly exchanges with strangers on the way.

name: Presence over performance
summary: Putting full attention on what's happening now rather than on planning the next line or judging yourself.
how_to_apply: When you notice yourself rehearsing, return attention to her words, her face, the setting; respond to what's actually said.
example_line: Wait, go back. You said 'technically' a lawyer?
markers: median_response_gap_s in normal range (not frozen, not jumping in)
drill: During one conversation, do a 1-second body check (feet, breath) whenever you catch yourself rehearsing.

name: Counter the liking gap
summary: Remembering that people usually like us more than we think after a conversation, so pessimism fuels needy behaviour.
how_to_apply: When you leave thinking it went badly, look for her objective engagement signals before concluding anything.
example_line: (Self-talk: what did she actually do?)
markers: her questions and turn length vs his own self-assessment
drill: After each recorded chat, rate how much she liked you (1-10) before the coach review, then compare to her engagement markers.

name: Rejection reframe
summary: Treating rejection as a sign you took a risk and a filter for fit, not as evidence of low worth.
how_to_apply: After a no, say something gracious, leave, and note what you'd keep doing; never argue or sulk.
example_line: No problem at all. Have a great night.
markers: response to a decline: brief, warm, no persuasion
common_mistakes: Pretending you don't care while sulking
drill: Collect three small rejections this month (ask for small favours or numbers) and practise the gracious exit.

name: Hold your frame without arguing
summary: Keeping your own calm reading of a situation when she challenges it, without needing her to agree.
how_to_apply: Restate your view briefly and good-humouredly once; don't stack justifications; move on.
example_line: Ha, maybe. I still think pineapple belongs on pizza. Anyway...
markers: justification length after a challenge (words in next turn)
back-pedalling phrases ('I mean, I didn't mean...')
common_mistakes: Turning 'frame' into dominance or arguing to win
Refusing to update when actually wrong
drill: When challenged in low-stakes chats, answer in one sentence max, then ask a question.
ethics_note: Frame control can slide into refusing to hear her view; the coach checks that Tom still listens and updates when she has a point.

name: Don't over-explain
summary: Cutting long justifications, which signal you need her approval of your choices.
how_to_apply: Give the reason in one clause or none; let silence do the rest.
example_line: I left finance because it bored me.
markers: turn length after 'why' questions vs baseline
drill: Answer five 'why' questions about your life in one sentence each; record and check.

name: Agree and amplify
summary: Responding to a playful jab by agreeing and exaggerating it until it's absurd, which shows it didn't land.
how_to_apply: Take the accusation, inflate it humorously, smile, move on.
example_line: Player? I have a spreadsheet. Colour-coded. You're row 412.
common_mistakes: Using it on sincere concerns (she might really be checking)
drill: Have a friend throw ten mock-accusations; answer each with agree-and-amplify, then with a sincere answer.

name: Sincere answer to sincere question
summary: Recognising when a 'test' is a real question about safety or values and answering it straight.
how_to_apply: If she asks about intentions, exes or safety, give a short honest answer without jokes.
example_line: Fair question. I'm looking for something real, not a string of dates.
markers: joke vs plain-answer to direct value questions
common_mistakes: Treating every question as a test to be beaten
drill: List three questions women often ask on early dates; write a one-line honest answer for each.

name: Pass the 'are you rattled?' check
summary: Staying relaxed when she teases or provokes, which practitioners say is the actual point of many tests.
how_to_apply: Don't flinch, don't sulk, don't overreact; a smile, a light line or a calm plain statement all pass.
example_line: You're trying to make me nervous. It's working a little.
markers: pitch_median_hz and speaking_rate_wpm stable after a provocation
drill: Notice the next three times you're teased; respond within two seconds with something light.

name: Reframe awkwardness as shared fun
summary: Turning an awkward moment into an in-joke, which removes its sting for both people.
how_to_apply: Name it lightly and make it 'ours'.
example_line: So that was the worst handshake in recorded history. We'll laugh about it later.
drill: In a week of chats, find two small awkward moments and name them out loud playfully.

name: Reframe the role: you're choosing too
summary: Shifting your internal frame from 'auditioning for her' to 'two people seeing if they fit'.
how_to_apply: Ask yourself during the date what you're learning about her values and whether you like them.
example_line: I'm curious, what's something you're stubborn about?
common_mistakes: Turning it into an interview or judging out loud
drill: Write three qualities you want in a partner; listen for evidence of them on your next date.

name: Slow down under pressure
summary: Deliberately lowering pace and pitch when stakes rise, countering the stress pattern of speeding up and pitching higher.
how_to_apply: When you notice adrenaline, breathe out, slow your next sentence and land it with a falling ending.
example_line: (Slowly) I'd like that.
markers: pitch_median_hz rise > 2 st vs relaxed baseline (heuristic flag)
drill: Record yourself telling the same story relaxed and then while standing in front of a friend; compare rate and pitch.

name: Comfortable silence
summary: Letting a pause sit for a couple of seconds without rushing to fill it.
how_to_apply: In lulls, count to two silently, smile, then say something light or ask a real question.
example_line: (Pause) ...You've got a story there, I can tell.
markers: who breaks silences and how fast (gaps)
silences 1-3 s not immediately filled by Tom
common_mistakes: Using silence as a power move to unsettle her
drill: In low-stakes chats, let one pause run to a slow count of three before you speak.

name: Amused tolerance
summary: Meeting friction, provocation or drama with warm amusement rather than anger or anxiety.
how_to_apply: Smile through it, keep tone warm, respond with lightness, and don't escalate.
example_line: You're a lot of trouble, you know that?
markers: no rise in loudness_db during disagreement
common_mistakes: Condescension (laughing at her rather than with the situation)
Using it to dismiss real concerns
drill: When you feel irritated in a conversation this week, choose one amused response before reacting.

sources.where: humour and love in the face of her tests

ethics_note: Red-pill 'amused mastery' is often framed as condescension toward women; the coach keeps only the warm, non-reactive version.

name: Keep your plans
summary: Not cancelling commitments or bending boundaries at the first sign of interest from her.
how_to_apply: Offer alternatives instead of dropping what you had planned.
example_line: I can't Friday, I've got the gig. Saturday works.
markers: proposals offered as alternatives rather than cancellations
drill: Next time someone asks for your time when you're busy, offer an alternative rather than cancelling.

name: Don't react to bait
summary: Choosing not to take the hook when someone (including other men) tries to provoke or one-up you.
how_to_apply: Acknowledge lightly or ignore; redirect to the group or to her.
example_line: Ha, fair enough. Anyway, you were saying about Porto?
markers: no escalation in loudness_db or interruptions after provocation
drill: When someone tries to one-up you this week, respond with genuine interest in their story instead.

name: Cocky-funny
summary: Combining exaggerated self-confidence with humour so it's obviously a joke, signalling ease without real arrogance.
how_to_apply: Say a cheeky, over-the-top line about yourself or the situation with a smile; keep the target safe and the warmth obvious.
example_line: Careful, I'm very charming after one coffee.
common_mistakes: Every line a bit; no sincerity
Cocky without funny or funny without cocky
drill: Write five over-the-top lines about your own charm; deliver each with a deadpan then a smile; keep the two that make friends laugh.

name: Mock accusation
summary: Playfully accusing her of something absurd (e.g. trying to seduce you, being a troublemaker) to create a fun dynamic.
how_to_apply: Pick a harmless, obviously untrue 'accusation' linked to something she just did; smile.
example_line: Are you hitting on me? I'm flattered, but I barely know you.
common_mistakes: Accusations about real flaws or sexual behaviour
drill: Use one mock accusation per conversation for a week; note when it lands and when it doesn't.

name: Role reversal
summary: Playfully treating yourself as the one being pursued or needing to be won over.
how_to_apply: Flip the usual script with a smile: you're the one being careful with her, she has to behave.
example_line: Slow down. I'm not that kind of guy... on a Tuesday.
drill: Write three role-reversal lines for common moments (she pays a compliment, she suggests a drink, she touches your arm).

name: Tease the safe stuff
summary: Teasing her about choices she's proud of or neutral things (her drink, her strong opinions), never insecurities.
how_to_apply: Tease, smile, and land on warmth within a turn or two.
example_line: Oat milk and three shots. You're clearly the chaotic one.
markers: warmth token after the tease ('I love that though')
common_mistakes: Teasing someone who isn't playing back
drill: For each tease you make this week, add a warm line within your next turn.

name: Tease back when teased
summary: Matching her playful challenges with your own, so the banter becomes two-way.
how_to_apply: Accept her jab with a smile and return one in the same register.
example_line: Says the woman who just admitted she irons her jeans.
drill: In banter, aim for at least two back-and-forth exchanges before shifting to sincere.

name: Tease, then sincere
summary: Alternating playful teasing with genuine appreciation so she knows the fun comes from liking her.
how_to_apply: After a run of banter, say one sincere specific compliment or ask a real question.
example_line: Okay, jokes aside, the way you talk about your sister is lovely.
markers: her disclosure increases after sincere turns
common_mistakes: Sincerity that feels like a tactic
drill: Practise 'three jokes, one sincere' in a conversation and note how she responds to the sincere beat.

name: Role-play premise
summary: Inventing a playful fictional scenario about the two of you, which builds 'we' and fun.
how_to_apply: Take a detail and spin it into a mini-scenario; invite her to add to it.
example_line: We'd be a terrible heist team. You'd stop for snacks mid-robbery.
common_mistakes: Forcing it when she's not playful
Running the bit for too long
drill: Pick three ordinary situations (queue, cooking, travel) and write one absurd 'us' premise for each.

name: Yes-and her bits
summary: Building on her joke rather than topping it with an unrelated one, the improv rule that creates co-created humour.
how_to_apply: When she says something playful, accept and extend it in the same direction.
example_line: She: 'I'd be a great pirate.' You: 'Obviously. You'd be the one who negotiates the treasure split.'
markers: his turn content extends her premise
common_mistakes: Stealing the spotlight with your own joke
drill: Count yes-and builds per conversation; aim to raise the number each week.

name: Playful misinterpretation
summary: Deliberately reading her innocent words as flirtatious or ridiculous, as an obvious joke.
how_to_apply: Pick up a double meaning, twist it lightly, then let it go.
example_line: So you're saying you want to see me again. Bold.
drill: Listen for one ambiguous phrase per conversation and twist it lightly.

name: Callback humour
summary: Bringing back an earlier detail or joke later, which shows attention and creates in-jokes.
how_to_apply: Note one funny or distinctive detail early; reuse it once or twice later.
example_line: ...which as a future pirate negotiator, you'd appreciate.
markers: references to earlier content after > 5 minutes
common_mistakes: Callbacks to something she didn't enjoy
drill: Note one detail in the first five minutes and call back to it later; review if it landed.

name: Nicknames and in-jokes
summary: Giving a playful, affectionate nickname based on something she said, creating a private shared world.
how_to_apply: Use a nickname tied to a specific moment, only if she responds warmly.
example_line: Alright, Captain Spreadsheet, where next?
markers: her reaction to the nickname (laughter vs flat)
drill: Try one moment-based nickname on a playful date; drop it if she doesn't smile.

name: Entertain yourself
summary: Saying things because they amuse you, not to get a reaction, which makes humour feel effortless.
how_to_apply: Follow your curiosity and comedic instinct; don't check her face after every line.
example_line: I've decided this pigeon is our waiter.
markers: laughter share: Tom laughs naturally but not at every own line
common_mistakes: Laughing at your own jokes when she doesn't
drill: On your next outing, say one thing purely because it amuses you, then let it go whatever her reaction.

name: Laugh off a missed joke
summary: Handling a joke that flops by acknowledging it lightly and moving on.
how_to_apply: Name it in under five words, smile, carry on.
example_line: Okay, that one died. Moving on.
drill: Deliberately tell a terrible pun to a friend and practise the five-word recovery.

name: Light challenge
summary: Playfully challenging her to earn your interest, e.g. questioning whether she's adventurous enough.
how_to_apply: Frame the challenge as a game with a smile, about an activity or taste, never her worth.
example_line: Wait, you've never had durian? I'm not sure we can be friends.
common_mistakes: Challenges about her looks or worth
drill: Write three playful 'can we be friends?' challenges about tastes; use one per date.
ethics_note: Only ethical if it's about tastes or activities and clearly playful; a challenge to her worth slides into negging.

name: Exaggeration
summary: Inflating small things to absurd proportions for comic effect.
how_to_apply: Take a mundane fact and treat it as epic.
example_line: Four trips to Lisbon? At this point you're legally Portuguese.
drill: Retell three boring facts about your week with one absurd exaggeration each.

name: Self-deprecation only from strength
summary: Using self-deprecating humour sparingly and about trivial things, since it helps mainly when status is already clear.
how_to_apply: Joke about small foibles, not core worth; keep it rare.
example_line: My cooking is mainly a fire safety exercise.
markers: count of self-deprecating remarks per conversation
drill: Audit a recording for self-deprecation; keep at most one trivial one.

name: Tease the situation, not the person
summary: Directing humour at the setting, the moment or shared absurdities, a lower-risk way to be playful.
how_to_apply: Comment wryly on the venue, the queue or the music.
example_line: This DJ is clearly going through something.
common_mistakes: Sneering at staff or other people
drill: Make one observational joke about the setting in the first two minutes of each conversation.

name: Slow, unhurried delivery
summary: Speaking at a relaxed, steady pace that suggests you're not worried about losing her attention.
how_to_apply: Slightly slower than your nervous pace; pause between ideas; don't rush endings.
example_line: (Measured) I've been thinking about that, actually.
markers: rushing = high rate + few pauses + rising ends
drill: Read a paragraph aloud at your normal pace, then with a breath after each sentence; compare.

name: Pause before the point
summary: A short pause before a key line, which adds weight and draws attention.
how_to_apply: Take a beat before punchlines, compliments and invitations.
example_line: You know what I like about you? (pause) You don't take yourself seriously.
markers: long_pauses immediately before a falling, fluent statement
drill: Mark three pause points in a story and practise hitting them.

name: Land statements with a downward inflection
summary: Ending statements on a falling pitch so they sound decided rather than asked.
how_to_apply: Drop your pitch on the last stressed word; stop talking.
example_line: Let's go to the one by the river.
common_mistakes: Misreading UK floor-holding rises as weakness
drill: Full-stop drill: five opinions, each with a clear fall and a one-second silence.

name: Replace fillers with silence
summary: Swapping 'um', 'like' and 'you know' for brief silent pauses.
how_to_apply: When you feel a filler coming, close your mouth and pause.
example_line: (Instead of 'Um, so, like, I...') So. I moved to London in 2019.
drill: Two-minute story drill: every filler replaced by silence; check fillers_per_100w.

name: Cut hedges from opinions
summary: Removing 'maybe', 'sort of', 'I guess' from opinions and plans, while keeping honest uncertainty when it's real.
how_to_apply: State the view plainly; if unsure, say 'my guess is' once rather than scattering hedges.
example_line: That film is overrated.
common_mistakes: Fake certainty about things you don't know
drill: Rewrite five of your recent text messages without hedges; read them aloud.

name: Vocal variety in stories
summary: Using a wider range of pitch, pace and volume when telling stories, which reads as charismatic.
how_to_apply: Lift energy in the exciting part, drop low and slow for the punchline or the personal bit.
example_line: (Building) ...and then the door opens, and (drops) it's my mum.
markers: pitch_range_st and loudness_sd_db in story turns vs neutral turns
drill: Tell the same 60-second story flat, then with deliberate variation; compare pitch_range_st.

name: Lower, softer voice for intimacy
summary: Dropping volume and slowing down when the conversation turns personal or flirtatious.
how_to_apply: When she shares something personal or you compliment her, lower volume and slow down.
example_line: (Quieter) I'm really glad you came out tonight.
markers: loudness_db drop in flirtatious stretches vs his networking baseline
drill: Practise one sincere compliment at normal volume then at 70%; ask a friend which felt warmer.

name: Warm tone: smile in the voice
summary: Letting warmth be audible (smiling while speaking, relaxed breath), balancing strength with friendliness.
how_to_apply: Smile slightly while greeting and asking questions; relax your jaw.
example_line: Hey! Good to see you.
drill: Record a greeting neutral and with a smile; listen for the difference.

name: Hold the floor gracefully
summary: Finishing your thought when lightly interrupted rather than immediately giving up the turn.
how_to_apply: Raise a hand or say 'one sec' and finish briefly; then hand over with a question.
example_line: Hang on, let me finish this bit, it's the best part.
drill: In group chats, finish one interrupted thought per evening, then hand over.

name: Project to be heard
summary: Speaking loudly enough for the setting, as quiet mumbled speech signals low confidence in noisy venues.
how_to_apply: Speak from the chest, aim your voice at her, adjust up in bars.
example_line: (Clear, audible opener in a loud bar.)
common_mistakes: Not adjusting down in quiet settings
drill: Count how many times you're asked to repeat yourself in a loud venue; aim for zero.

name: Full attention, quick fitting responses
summary: Responding promptly and on-topic, which signals engagement; fast, fitting replies track 'clicking'.
how_to_apply: Listen fully; let your reply come from what she said, not a prepared line.
example_line: Wait, you quit on your first day?
drill: In one conversation, make every reply begin with a word she just used.

name: Don't rush to answer compliments or questions
summary: Taking a breath before answering charged questions or compliments, rather than rushing to deflect.
how_to_apply: Accept a compliment with 'thank you' and a pause; answer personal questions after a beat.
example_line: (Pause) Thank you. That's nice to hear.
common_mistakes: Overly long pauses that read as cold
drill: Accept the next five compliments you get with only 'thank you' and a smile.

name: Decisive yes/no answers
summary: Answering simple questions directly instead of with waffling.
how_to_apply: Lead with yes, no or a choice; add reason only if needed.
example_line: Red. Definitely red.
markers: latency and hedges on simple preference questions
drill: For a day, answer every simple preference question with a choice in the first word.

name: Presence-power-warmth balance
summary: Charisma as a mix of presence (attention), power (capability) and warmth (goodwill); missing one makes the others read worse.
how_to_apply: Check each conversation: was I present, did I sound capable, did I sound kind?
example_line: (Not a line: a self-check.)
common_mistakes: Power without warmth (reads as cold or arrogant)
Warmth without power (reads as nice guy)
drill: After each recording, score yourself 1-5 on presence, power and warmth; compare with the coach's read.

name: Hook, tension, payoff
summary: Telling stories with a clear opening hook, a moment of tension and a payoff, which research links to men's attractiveness and status.
how_to_apply: Open with the most intriguing line, build to one obstacle, deliver the payoff, stop.
example_line: I once got locked in a museum overnight. Worth it, mostly.
markers: her reaction at the payoff (laughter, questions)
common_mistakes: Burying the hook at the end
drill: Write your three best stories as hook / tension / payoff in three lines each; tell each in under 90 seconds.

name: Keep it short
summary: Trimming stories to their essential beats so the other person stays engaged and gets a turn.
how_to_apply: Aim for under about 90 seconds (heuristic); cut background she doesn't need.
example_line: (A tight 60-second version of a travel story.)
markers: longest_turn_s and mean_turn_s vs her turns
her interruptions or backchannels fading during his story
common_mistakes: Cutting so much there's no detail
drill: Time your go-to story; cut it by a third without losing the payoff.

name: Paint the scene
summary: Using concrete images, dialogue and feelings so she can picture the moment.
how_to_apply: Include one sensory detail and one line of dialogue in each story.
example_line: The man in the hat just looked at me and said, 'You're in the wrong country, mate.'
markers: concrete nouns and quoted speech in story turns
drill: Retell yesterday as a story with one smell, one sound and one quote.

name: Demonstrate, don't declare
summary: Letting qualities like competence, courage or kindness come out through what happened, not by stating them.
how_to_apply: Choose stories where the trait is visible in your actions; never add 'I'm a pretty adventurous guy'.
example_line: I'd never sailed, but the skipper broke his wrist, so I learnt fast.
drill: Rewrite one 'I'm the kind of guy who...' claim as a 20-second story.

name: Character over credentials
summary: Choosing stories that reveal values and emotions (curiosity, loyalty, fear overcome) rather than income or achievements.
how_to_apply: Pick stories where something mattered to you emotionally.
example_line: The best day of that trip was teaching my nephew to swim.
drill: List five stories; mark each as 'credential' or 'character'; lead with character ones.

sources.where: women connect with appreciation and focus on them

name: Match and step up disclosure
summary: Sharing personal information at roughly the same depth as her, then going slightly deeper, which builds closeness.
how_to_apply: After she shares, share something comparable; occasionally go one notch deeper.
example_line: That's a big move. I nearly did the same thing after my dad got ill.
markers: disclosure depth of his turn vs her previous turn
drill: Practise the Aron-style progression with a friend: three question sets of increasing depth.

name: Stories that invite hers
summary: Ending a story with a hook that naturally invites her to share a similar experience.
how_to_apply: Finish with a beat or a light question tied to the theme.
example_line: ...so that's my worst travel story. I bet yours is better.
markers: her next turn length and whether she tells a story
common_mistakes: Mechanically asking 'what about you?' after everything
drill: Add a natural invitation to the end of each of your three best stories.

name: Use 'you' and 'we' in stories
summary: Pulling her into the story by relating it to her or to an imagined shared future.
how_to_apply: Connect a story to something she said, or end with 'we should...'.
example_line: You'd have loved it. You'd have negotiated us a free dinner.
drill: For one story, add a line that links it to her.

name: Open threads in stories
summary: Leaving interesting loose details she can ask about, which hands her easy ways in.
how_to_apply: Mention a curious detail without explaining it fully.
example_line: That was the summer I lived on a boat. Anyway...
markers: her questions about details he dropped
common_mistakes: Teasing details then refusing to explain (feels manipulative)
drill: Drop one unexplained interesting detail per conversation and see if she picks it up.

name: Avoid humblebrags
summary: Not dressing up boasts as complaints, which lowers liking more than straight bragging.
how_to_apply: Either state the fact plainly when relevant or leave it out.
example_line: (Instead of 'Ugh, so tired of all these work trips to Tokyo') I go to Tokyo for work a lot. Love it.
common_mistakes: Hiding every achievement out of fear
drill: Scan a recording for humblebrags; restate any as plain facts.

name: Follow-up questions
summary: Asking questions that build on what she just said; the strongest research-backed liking behaviour in early conversations.
how_to_apply: Take a word from her answer and ask about it, two levels deep before switching topic.
example_line: You said 'technically' a nurse. What's the non-technical version?
markers: questions classified as follow-up vs switch
her answer length after his questions
drill: Two-deep rule: two follow-ups on any interesting answer before changing topic.

name: Statements instead of questions
summary: Making observations or guesses about her instead of asking interview questions, which creates more engaging conversation.
how_to_apply: Turn 'where are you from?' into a guess: 'You seem like you grew up by the sea.'
example_line: You seem like the friend who organises the group holiday.
markers: ratio of 'you seem/you strike me' statements to closed questions
common_mistakes: Guesses that are insults in disguise
drill: Convert five standard first-date questions into playful statements.

name: Playful cold read
summary: Making a perceptive but general guess about her personality; it often feels accurate because of the Barnum effect.
how_to_apply: Base it on something she actually said; frame it as a guess; be curious if wrong.
example_line: I'm guessing you're social, but you need your alone time to recharge.
markers: her response: confirms and elaborates vs corrects
common_mistakes: Using reads to fake deep connection
drill: Practise three reads on friends from observed details only; note accuracy.
ethics_note: Cold reads work partly through a cognitive bias; keep them as light, openly-guessing curiosity, never to manufacture a false sense of special connection.

name: Label the feeling
summary: Naming the emotion behind what she's describing, which shows understanding.
how_to_apply: Use 'sounds like...' or 'seems like...' plus the feeling, then pause.
example_line: Sounds like that job made you feel invisible.
drill: In three conversations, make one emotional label each and note her response.

name: Appreciation and sympathy
summary: Specific appreciation ('that's brilliant') and sympathy ('that must have been hard') made women feel connected in speed-date research.
how_to_apply: Respond to good news with specific appreciation and to hard news with sympathy before moving on.
example_line: That must have been brutal. And you still finished the course?
drill: Replace every 'cool' in a conversation with a specific reaction.

name: Collaborative completion
summary: Briefly finishing or adding to her sentence to show you're following, which signalled understanding in speed dates.
how_to_apply: Use sparingly when you clearly get where she's going.
example_line: She: 'And I just thought, why am I even...' You: '...still there.'
markers: overlaps that complete her thought (cooperative interruptions)
drill: Listen for one moment per chat where a short completion fits.

name: Threading
summary: Picking one of several hooks in her answer to continue, so the conversation never hits a dead end.
how_to_apply: Listen for 2-3 hooks in each answer; follow the most emotional or unusual one.
example_line: Wait, back up, the circus part?
markers: topic continuity; dead-end count (long gaps followed by new unrelated topic)
drill: Listen to a podcast interview; pause after each answer and list three hooks.

name: Go from facts to feelings
summary: Shifting questions from what she does to why, how it felt and what she wants.
how_to_apply: After a fact, ask about the motivation or emotion behind it.
example_line: What made you pick nursing over medicine?
markers: share of why/how/feel questions after 10 minutes
drill: For each fact she gives, ask one 'why' or 'what was that like'.

sources.where: deeper conversations less awkward than expected

name: Deep but light questions
summary: Asking more interesting questions than small talk, delivered playfully, since people underestimate how much strangers enjoy depth.
how_to_apply: Swap 'what do you do?' for 'what are you excited about at the moment?'
example_line: What's something you're weirdly good at?
drill: Prepare five 'deep but light' questions and rotate them.

name: Language and energy matching
summary: Converging with her style of speech, energy and vocabulary; style matching predicts relationship initiation.
how_to_apply: Notice her pace, energy and favourite words; meet her nearer to them.
example_line: (She's quiet and wry; you drop your volume and use dry humour.)
markers: speaking_rate_wpm and loudness_db convergence across the conversation
drill: Review a recording: where did your energies diverge? Practise one adjustment.

name: Mirror her last words
summary: Repeating the last few key words she said with a curious tone, prompting her to expand.
how_to_apply: Repeat 1-3 words, slight upward tone, then wait.
example_line: She: 'I just got back from Peru.' You: 'Peru?'
markers: his turn echoes her final words
drill: Use three mirrors in a low-stakes chat; count how long she talks after each.

name: Focus the conversation on her
summary: Keeping much of the topical focus on her life and views; both sexes reported more 'click' when talk centred on the woman.
how_to_apply: Return the spotlight to her after your stories; don't let it drift into your résumé.
example_line: Enough about me. What's the thing you'd do if money didn't matter?
drill: Review a recording and mark whose life each topic was about.

sources.where: talk in terms of their interests

name: Don't make her carry it
summary: Taking responsibility for keeping conversation flowing so she isn't forced to ask all the questions.
how_to_apply: If she's asked two questions in a row, ask one back or offer a story.
example_line: (After she asks twice) Okay, my turn to be nosy.
drill: Track the question ratio in your next three recordings.

sources.where: women disconnected when they had to ask

name: Use her name and specifics
summary: Using her name and specific details she shared, which makes her feel noticed.
how_to_apply: Use her name once or twice; refer back to specifics.
example_line: Sophie, you've ruined all other coffee for me.
drill: Use the name of three new people in conversation this week.

name: Ask about her passions
summary: Steering towards what lights her up, so her emotional state during the conversation is positive and associated with you.
how_to_apply: Listen for energy spikes in her voice and ask more there.
example_line: You lit up when you mentioned the band. Tell me about that.
markers: her pitch_range_st and loudness rise in her turns
her turn length on that topic
common_mistakes: Ignoring topics she enjoys to return to yours
drill: In a recording, find her highest-energy moment and note whether you followed it.

name: Find commonalities, then differ playfully
summary: Building rapport through genuine shared interests, then adding contrast so it isn't bland agreement.
how_to_apply: Note a real shared thing; enjoy it; then playfully disagree on a detail.
example_line: We both love Japan. But you're wrong about the ramen.
markers: 'me too' moments followed by playful divergence
drill: Look for one genuine commonality and one playful disagreement per date.

name: Validate before disagreeing
summary: Acknowledging her perspective before offering a different one, keeping warmth and frame.
how_to_apply: 'I see why you'd think that' then your view.
example_line: Fair, I get why people love it. For me it's a bit much.
drill: In the next disagreement, validate first in one sentence.

name: Make intent clear
summary: Signalling romantic rather than friendly interest so you don't drift into the friend zone and she can respond honestly.
how_to_apply: Once rapport is there, say something clearly romantic once, warmly, and see how she responds.
example_line: I'm enjoying this more than I expected. You're trouble.
markers: presence of an explicit or clearly romantic statement
drill: In your next date, say one clearly romantic line before the halfway point.

sources.where: women want men to show interest

name: Specific compliment on character
summary: One sincere compliment about something she chose (a story, a view, her style), said once and left alone.
how_to_apply: Make it specific, say it calmly, don't wait for a reaction.
example_line: I like how you talk about your work. You actually care.
markers: compliments: specific vs generic, looks vs choices
common_mistakes: Compliment as opener for a request
drill: One specific choice-based compliment per date, then drop it.

name: Escalate in step with her
summary: Gradually moving to more personal and flirtatious topics only after signs she's enjoying it.
how_to_apply: After each step, read her next three turns; continue if she matches, step back if she pulls away.
example_line: (After she teases back) So what's your type, then? Besides dangerously charming.
markers: her turn length, questions and laughter after each step
drill: After each escalation, check her next three turns in the recording.

name: Flirty subtext, not explicit content
summary: Letting flirtation live in implication and playfulness rather than explicit sexual talk early on.
how_to_apply: Hint, imply, let her fill the gap; keep it deniable and light.
example_line: You should probably stop looking at me like that. People will talk.
drill: Rewrite three blunt flirty lines as subtext.
ethics_note: Only appropriate when she's reciprocating; persisting with innuendo she ignores is pressure.

name: Tension and release
summary: Alternating playful challenge or teasing with warmth, giving the conversation emotional rhythm.
how_to_apply: After a playful jab or disagreement, follow with appreciation; keep both honest.
example_line: You're a terrible influence. I like it.
markers: alternation of teasing and warm turns
drill: Write five lines that pair a playful challenge with a compliment.
ethics_note: Ethical only as playful conversational rhythm; deliberately alternating approval and withdrawal to create anxiety is manipulative (see off-limits push-pull).

name: Let tension sit
summary: Not defusing every charged moment with a joke or nervous chatter.
how_to_apply: When a moment feels charged, hold it for a beat before speaking.
example_line: (Pause, smile) ...What?
markers: nervous laughter by Tom after charged moments
common_mistakes: Prolonged staring silence that's uncomfortable for her
drill: Next charged moment, count one breath before responding.

name: Keep your edges
summary: Maintaining your own views and direction rather than merging into constant agreement; difference keeps attraction alive.
how_to_apply: Disagree warmly, keep your own interests visible, don't mirror everything she says.
example_line: I see it differently, actually.
drill: Notice your agreement rate in a recording; aim for honest agreement only.
ethics_note: Deida's masculine/feminine polarity is untested and essentialist; the coach keeps only the behaviour (stable identity, calm difference).

name: Keep some mystery
summary: Not revealing everything at once; letting her discover you over time.
how_to_apply: Answer honestly but not exhaustively; leave some stories for later.
example_line: That's a story for the second date.
markers: his disclosure volume early vs later
common_mistakes: Evasiveness or secrecy that feels deceptive
drill: Pick one good story you'll save for a later date.

name: Future projection
summary: Playfully imagining future shared scenarios, which builds 'we' and romantic frame.
how_to_apply: Light, obviously playful 'we' futures, not commitment talk.
example_line: When we go to Japan, you're in charge of the itinerary.
common_mistakes: Sounding needy or serious too early
drill: Use one playful future projection on your next date.
ethics_note: Keep it obviously playful; using false future promises to secure intimacy is deception.

name: Express attraction directly and calmly
summary: Saying you find her attractive in a relaxed, specific way, rather than hiding behind jokes.
how_to_apply: Say it once, calmly, without asking for a response.
example_line: You look really good tonight.
drill: Practise one calm, direct compliment with a friend until it feels natural.

name: Playful disqualification
summary: Joking that you two could never work, which creates playful tension when interest is already clear.
how_to_apply: Use only when rapport and mutual interest are obvious; keep it absurd.
example_line: This would never work. You like Marmite.
common_mistakes: Using it when she's unsure (reads as rejection)
drill: Pair a playful disqualification with a warm comment.
ethics_note: Keep it obviously playful and pair it with warmth; using it to make her chase or doubt herself is manipulative.

name: Desire needs separateness (long-term)
summary: In relationships, maintaining individual lives, interests and some novelty sustains desire.
how_to_apply: Keep your own passions; talk about them with energy; plan new experiences together.
example_line: I'm off to the climbing trip this weekend. Tell me about yours when I'm back.
drill: Name one solo pursuit to maintain and one novel shared activity per month.

name: Default plus easy out
summary: Proposing a specific plan while giving her an easy way to decline or adjust.
how_to_apply: Name day, place and activity; add a light 'unless you'd rather...'.
example_line: Thursday, the wine bar on Exmouth Market. Unless you've a better idea.
markers: specific proposals vs vague ('we should hang out')
drill: Phrase every suggestion this week as a concrete default with an easy exit.

name: Lead without asking permission at every step
summary: Moving things along (next topic, next drink, leaving) with light assertive statements instead of repeated check-ins.
how_to_apply: Suggest, don't poll; still read her reaction.
example_line: Let's grab food. I know a place.
markers: 'let's' statements vs 'do you want to maybe' questions
drill: Use 'let's' for three small decisions on your next outing.

name: Move on when energy dips
summary: Switching topic, activity or venue before the conversation goes flat.
how_to_apply: When answers shorten, change topic or suggest moving.
example_line: Right, we've solved politics. Dessert?
drill: In a recording, find the first energy dip and note how long you took to shift.

name: Smooth transitions
summary: Changing topics with a link or a light marker so it feels natural.
how_to_apply: Bridge with a word from the last topic or a playful 'random question'.
example_line: Speaking of terrible decisions, have you ever done karaoke?
markers: topic transitions with bridges vs abrupt
drill: Practise three bridges in a chat with a friend.

name: Choose when asked
summary: Making the choice when she says 'you pick', which takes the planning burden off her.
how_to_apply: Pick quickly and say why in a few words.
example_line: Thai. They do a ridiculous green curry.
markers: response latency and hedges after 'you choose'
common_mistakes: Choosing and ignoring her stated preferences
drill: Next time someone says 'you choose', decide within three seconds.

name: Ask clearly
summary: Asking for a date or number directly, without hedging or disguising it as something else.
how_to_apply: Name what you want and a plan: 'I'd like to take you out. Saturday?'
example_line: I'd like to see you again. Saturday, a drink?
drill: End your next three good conversations with a clear ask.

name: Accept the answer gracefully
summary: Taking any answer, including no or maybe, lightly and without persuasion.
how_to_apply: Respond warmly and move on; a maybe is not a yes to chase.
example_line: No problem. It was lovely meeting you.
drill: Role-play three declines with a friend, answering each in one gracious line.

name: End on a high
summary: Leaving or wrapping up while energy is good, rather than letting it fade.
how_to_apply: When things peak, propose the next step and wrap up.
example_line: I've got to head off, but this was great. Let's do Thursday.
markers: closing timing relative to her engagement peak
drill: Notice the peak moment of your next date and close within 15 minutes of it.

name: Set the frame early
summary: Establishing the tone (playful, curious, warm) in the first minute, which tends to carry through.
how_to_apply: Open with an easy, positive, slightly playful line that sets the mood.
example_line: Okay, important question before we start: sweet or savoury breakfast?
drill: Prepare three situational openers and use one per day for a week.

name: Verbal indicators of interest
summary: Recognising audible signs she's interested: her questions, longer answers, laughter, 'we' talk, her own teasing.
how_to_apply: Check these before escalating; treat them as a running total, not one signal.
example_line: (Not a line: a read.)
drill: After each recording, estimate her interest, then compare with these counts.

name: Spot disinterest early
summary: Noticing short answers, no questions back, topic changes or attempts to leave, and stepping back.
how_to_apply: When two or more signs appear, de-escalate or offer an easy exit.
example_line: Anyway, I'll let you get back to your friends. Nice meeting you.
drill: Mark the moment in a recording where her engagement dropped; note your next move.

name: Respect her signals over your plan
summary: Prioritising her responses over any technique or plan; a calibrated man adjusts.
how_to_apply: If something doesn't land, drop it.
example_line: (Drops the bit and asks a sincere question.)
markers: continuing a tactic after negative response
drill: Review one recording: list where you persisted with a bit that wasn't landing.

name: Match her energy level
summary: Adjusting your energy to slightly above hers, not wildly higher or lower.
how_to_apply: If she's calm, slow down; if she's lively, lift up.
example_line: (Brings energy down to match her quiet mood.)
drill: In a recording, compare your rate and loudness with hers in the first 5 minutes.

name: Repair a joke that offended
summary: Acknowledging quickly and sincerely when a joke hurt, without grovelling.
how_to_apply: One sincere line, then move on.
example_line: That came out wrong. Sorry, I didn't mean it that way.
drill: Practise a one-line repair for three plausible misfires.

name: Recover from awkward silences
summary: Using a light observation or callback to restart after a lull, without panic.
how_to_apply: Have a few easy re-starters: observation, callback, playful question.
example_line: Okay, so the pigeon situation is escalating.
drill: Keep three re-starters in mind for your next outing.

name: Win the group
summary: Engaging her friends warmly and including everyone, rather than isolating her.
how_to_apply: Address the group first; be friendly to everyone; don't rush to separate her.
example_line: So how do you all know each other?
drill: In group settings, make sure each person has spoken to you at least once.
ethics_note: Treating friends as 'obstacles' to neutralise is manipulative framing; the coach keeps only genuine inclusion.

name: Include, don't compete
summary: Responding to other men in the group with friendliness rather than competing or putting them down.
how_to_apply: Be friendly, share the spotlight, praise others' stories.
example_line: Ha, that's a better story than mine.
drill: Praise one other person's story in your next group chat.

name: Check your read (projection bias)
summary: Knowing that people mainly project their own intentions when guessing whether someone's flirting.
how_to_apply: Check her behaviour, not your feelings, before concluding she's interested.
example_line: (Self-check.)
markers: his self-rating vs her objective signals
drill: Rate her interest before the coach review and compare with her signals.

name: Context-appropriate humour
summary: Adjusting humour type and intensity to the setting and her personality.
how_to_apply: Gentler humour with serious or reserved people; bolder in playful settings.
example_line: (Swaps cocky lines for warm observational humour with a reserved date.)
drill: Track which kind of humour gets laughs in which settings.

name: Offer an easy out
summary: Giving her a graceful way to end or decline, which lowers pressure and often increases comfort.
how_to_apply: Make it easy for her to leave, decline or change her mind.
example_line: No pressure. If you'd rather call it a night, totally fine.
markers: exit offers present at escalation points
common_mistakes: Offering it in a passive-aggressive way
drill: At each escalation point, include one easy-out phrase.

name: Prestige, not dominance
summary: Gaining status through competence, generosity and humour rather than intimidation; women in studies prefer prestige.
how_to_apply: Share expertise generously; never put others down to rise.
example_line: If you're into photography I can show you a trick for night shots.
drill: Share one useful piece of expertise per week without being asked twice.

name: Pre-selection without bragging
summary: Being seen as socially valued (friends, warm greetings) can raise appeal; mention social life naturally, not as a boast.
how_to_apply: Mention friends and social life casually where relevant; never list women.
example_line: My friend Anna, who's a chef, dragged me there.
drill: Notice whether your stories include other people; add one where natural.
ethics_note: Mentioning other women to make her jealous or insecure is manipulative; the coach keeps only natural mention of a social life.

name: Screen for compatibility
summary: Asking questions that reveal her values and whether she fits what you want.
how_to_apply: Ask about things that matter to you (ambition, kindness, humour) with curiosity.
example_line: What's something you'd never compromise on?
drill: Write your top three partner values and one question for each.

name: Appreciate good answers
summary: When she shows a quality you value, say so, which signals you have standards and makes her feel seen.
how_to_apply: Name the quality simply.
example_line: I like that. You actually follow through on things.
drill: Once per date, appreciate a quality she shows.
ethics_note: Qualifying should be genuine; making her jump through hoops to win approval slides into manipulation.

name: Calm boundaries
summary: Saying no or naming disrespect calmly and briefly, without lecturing or punishing.
how_to_apply: State the boundary in one sentence; move on or leave if it's crossed again.
example_line: I'm not up for that. Let's do something else.
drill: Practise three boundary sentences aloud for common situations.

name: Don't tolerate flaking or disrespect silently
summary: Responding to repeated cancellations or rudeness by lowering investment, not pleading.
how_to_apply: Respond briefly and warmly, then let her re-initiate.
example_line: No worries. Let me know when you're free.
markers: pleading or rescheduling pressure in messages
drill: When someone flakes, reply once, warmly, and leave the next move to them.

name: Match her investment
summary: Keeping your effort roughly in step with hers, so you don't over-pursue.
how_to_apply: Notice who asks more questions, initiates more, compliments more.
example_line: (Not a line: a pattern.)
drill: In a recording, compare your and her questions and compliments.

name: Don't over-compliment
summary: Limiting compliments so each one means something, since gushing reads as unselective.
how_to_apply: One or two specific compliments per date.
example_line: (One compliment, well placed.)
drill: Count your compliments in a recording; keep the best one or two.

name: Accept compliments simply
summary: Taking compliments with a thank you rather than deflecting or bragging.
how_to_apply: Thank you, smile, maybe return the warmth.
example_line: Thanks. That's nice of you.
drill: Accept five compliments this week with just 'thank you'.

name: Plain facts, no humblebrag
summary: Stating achievements plainly when relevant, not hiding or overselling them.
how_to_apply: Say it once, matter-of-factly, then return to her.
example_line: I run a small software company. It's fun.
drill: Write a one-line plain description of your work and practise it.

name: Don't seek reassurance
summary: Not asking her to confirm she's having a good time or likes you.
how_to_apply: Trust the signals; if unsure, read her behaviour.
example_line: (Instead of 'Are you having fun? Is this okay?') —
markers: reassurance requests ('are you having fun?', 'do you like me?')
common_mistakes: Never checking comfort when it matters
drill: Count reassurance requests in a recording; cut to zero except genuine comfort checks.

name: Negging
summary: Backhanded compliments or mild put-downs meant to lower her confidence so she seeks your approval.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: affectionate teasing about safe topics, followed by warmth.
example_line: (Flag example) Nice hair, is it real?
markers: comments on looks with a put-down twist
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Designed to lower self-esteem; no peer-reviewed support and contrary to humour research.

name: Disqualifying her looks
summary: Openly suggesting she's not attractive enough to interest you, to unsettle her.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: honest, selective interest.
example_line: (Flag example) You're not usually my type.
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Manipulates self-worth.

name: Overriding last-minute resistance
summary: Treating her hesitation or no as something to get past.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: stop, check in, respect the answer.
example_line: (Flag) Come on, we're both adults...
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Coercive; ignores consent.

name: Persistence after a decline
summary: Repeatedly asking or arguing after she has said no.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: accept the answer gracefully.
example_line: (Flag) Just one drink, why not?
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Pressure; undermines consent.

name: Pressing drinks
summary: Encouraging her to drink more to lower inhibitions.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: let her set her own pace.
example_line: (Flag) Have another, it's on me.
markers: repeated offers of alcohol after she declines
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Exploits impaired judgement.

name: Isolating her
summary: Steering her away from her friends to remove social support.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: include her friends; propose moving only with her clear yes.
example_line: (Flag) Let's lose your friends.
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Removes her safety net.

name: Verbal escalation ignoring her cues
summary: Continuing sexual or intimate talk when she shows discomfort.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: step back at the first sign of discomfort.
example_line: (Flag) Continued innuendo after she changes subject.
markers: innuendo after topic change or short replies
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Ignores consent cues.

name: False time constraint
summary: Claiming you have to leave soon to lower her guard, without meaning it.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: be honest about your time.
example_line: (Flag) I can only stay a minute (stays an hour).
markers: stated time limit contradicted by conduct
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Deceptive.

name: Invented stories and fake personas
summary: Telling fabricated stories or claiming false credentials to impress.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: true stories told well.
example_line: (Flag) Pretending to be a pilot.
markers: claims Tom has said are untrue
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Deception.

name: Embedded commands and NLP patterns
summary: Covertly inserting suggestive phrases to influence her feelings without awareness.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: direct, honest expression.
example_line: (Flag) 'Imagine how it feels when you... melt into...'
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Covert influence; also unsupported by evidence.

name: Fake cold-read 'psychic' connection
summary: Using Barnum statements to make her believe you understand her uniquely.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: openly playful guesses.
example_line: (Flag) 'I can tell you've been hurt deeply.'
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Exploits a cognitive bias to create false intimacy.

name: Push-pull to unsettle
summary: Alternating approval and rejection specifically to create anxiety and chase.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: honest tension-and-release with consistent warmth.
example_line: (Flag) 'You're great... actually never mind, I'm off.'
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Uses anxiety to drive attraction.

name: Dread game
summary: Hinting she could lose you to other women to keep her insecure.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: secure, honest commitment and a full life of your own.
example_line: (Flag) 'That girl at work keeps texting me.'
markers: mentions of other women designed to provoke jealousy
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
ethics_note: Manufactures insecurity.

name: Freeze-outs and silent treatment
summary: Withdrawing warmth to punish or control.
how_to_apply: Do not use. Ethical alternative: calm, direct boundary statements.
example_line: (Flag) Sudden cold, one-word replies after she disagrees.
markers: abrupt warmth withdrawal after her disagreement
drill: Coach flags it; Tom practises the ethical alternative instead.
